title: Lees and bâtonnage
what: What happens to the fine yeast sediment after fermentation: leave the wine on it, rack the wine off it, or keep it and stir it back up (bâtonnage).

steps: so sulphury, reduced smells build up; stirring mixes in oxygen and prevents them

choose: Keep stirred fine lees for a barrel-aged Burgundy-style Chardonnay: the wine gains a richer, rounder texture, oak and oxygen are softened, and over months subtle bread or biscuit notes appear. Just how lees build texture is still debated. Rack off for a pure, fruit-led Riesling, or when the wine smells reduced.
exam: Questions ask how lees ageing and stirring change a white wine. Give autolysis → mannoproteins → richer texture and stability, the subtle bread note, fine against heavy lees, the reduction risk and stirring, and a region.

check.question: A Chardonnay sits unstirred on heavy lees in a large steel tank and starts to smell of rotten egg and drains. What helps most?
options: Stir the lees or rack the wine off them
Add SO₂: it binds the rotten-egg smell
Leave it: the smell always fades on lees
Move it into new oak to mask the smell
check.answer: Stir the lees or rack the wine off them
check.why: Settled lees are strongly reductive. Stirring mixes oxygen back in and racking removes the source; SO₂ or masking leaves the cause in place.

simplification: Game simplification: unstirred lees only slow the fading of H₂S already formed; haze and tartrate stability are not modelled; months on lees add body.
